summary: Punta Gorda Light, on California's Lost Coast, was first lit on 15 January 1912 and went dark in 1951; its concrete tower stands in the King Range, reached by a beach hike.

lens.note: Fourth-order lens; LighthouseFriends says the Fresnel lens was removed after the station closed.

structures.note: Iron lantern room atop a flat-roofed concrete base (NRHP).

access.note: On Bureau of Land Management land in the King Range National Conservation Area; reached by beach hike of just over three miles from Mattole Beach, with tide and creek hazards (LighthouseFriends).

visit.note: Interior open to visitors per LighthouseFriends; check trail and tide conditions with the BLM.

facts.agency: Bureau of Land Management (King Range National Conservation Area)

events.note: Compressed-air sirens driven by gasoline engines first sounded 22 June 1911.
Reinforced-concrete light tower completed, 27 ft (8.2 m).
Light first shown 15 January 1912: fourth-order lens, oil-vapour lamp, about 96,000 candlepower.
Earthquake (LighthouseFriends: 22 January 1923, 1:08 a.m.); quarters' foundation cracked, mercury shaken out, oil spilled.
Shocks on 9 January 1924 shook out the mercury, broke the mantle and, in one shock, stopped the lens.
Two severe shocks reported on 11 December (Bulletin 1931 volume); lens thrown out of adjustment, some mercury spilled.
Light extinguished 15 February 1951 (nomination); station decommissioned May 1951 (LighthouseFriends).
Property passed from the Coast Guard to the BLM on 16 January 1963 (nomination). LighthouseFriends says control passed in 1951: the sources disagree.
BLM burned the wooden buildings (LighthouseFriends: 1970; nomination: late 1960s).
Placed on the National Register of Historic Places (LighthouseFriends).
State conservation corps restored and painted the structures (LighthouseFriends).
Surviving structures rehabilitated in 2022-2023 under the Great American Outdoors Act; new circular staircase (LighthouseFriends).

wrecks.date_note: Nomination gives 12 July 1907; LighthouseFriends 21 July; the San Francisco Call of 23 July reports a collision at midnight on Saturday night, which is the night of 20-21 July.
wrecks.outcome: Passenger steamer sank after collision with the steam schooner San Pedro about 20 miles south of Point Gorda. Toll: 77 (nomination), 87 (LighthouseFriends); the San Francisco Call's latest advices put the survivors at 139.
Ran aground in heavy fog; a boiler and other pieces remain in the surf in front of the station.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The San Francisco Call of 23 July 1907 says the Columbia sank at midnight on Saturday night, 20 miles south of Point Gorda. That night runs into Sunday 21 July, the date LighthouseFriends gives; the nomination's 12 July does not fit the newspaper.

notes_for_editor:
1. Columbia: the date and toll disagree. Nomination: 12 July 1907, 77 lives. LighthouseFriends: 21 July 1907, 87 lives. San Francisco Call, 23 July 1907: sank at midnight on Saturday night; the paper's latest advices put survivors at 139. Its missing count is garbled in the OCR and is not used. The final toll is not settled by the sources read here and is not stated as settled in the story.
2. Light's end: the nomination gives extinguishment on 15 Feb 1951; LighthouseFriends gives decommissioning in May 1951. Both are used; the event is recorded as deactivated 1951.
3. Property: the nomination says the Coast Guard held the station until 16 Jan 1963, then the BLM; LighthouseFriends says the BLM had control from 1951. Unresolved; the story says the sources disagree.
4. Burning of the wooden buildings: nomination 'late 1960s', LighthouseFriends 1970.
5. Walk length: the 1975 nomination gives 4.5 miles; LighthouseFriends (current visitor notes) gives just over three miles.
6. Range: the nomination says the light was visible for 14 miles without stating a unit; range_nm is not set because the sources do not say nautical miles. The record has no range.
7. Keepers: all 45 USLHS roster lines are included with their archive person slugs. The USCG lines are recorded as role other because the archive gives no position. Evenden: roster 1944-45 vs nomination officer in charge 1943-45, both kept.
8. Earthquake of 1923: the Bulletin gives 1:08 a.m. and the 1923 volume; the date 22 January is from LighthouseFriends. The 1931 earthquake date (11 December) is read from the 1931 volume, which is not dated more precisely in the text read; the 1931 passage is OCR-damaged, so its wording is paraphrased.
9. The record's tower height of 8.0 m is close to the nomination's 27 ft (8.2 m); not corrected.
10. Harrington's father is named only as head keeper at Trinidad Head (LighthouseFriends); no name, so no other_stations entry.
11. No Humboldt newspaper search was run for the 1911-12 opening or the 1951 closure; the Chronicling America search was run for the Columbia only.
12. 1931 Bulletin (PDF page 10, printed page 61): the OCR of the lens sentence is garbled. The page image reads 'throwing the lens in the tower out of time and spilling some of the mercury'; the story uses 'out of time' from the image. The evidence quotes use only the clean OCR words.
13. 1891 report: the Punta Gorda passage is on scan page 219, printed page 160 (between the running heads for pages 159 and 161), in the 1891 report. Scan page 566 in the same volume holds a later report ('last three annual reports').
14. Keeper roster lines were compared with the cached archive page (archives.uslhs.org/places/punta-gorda); no line disagrees.
15. Walk length: the story gives both the 1975 nomination (4.5 miles) and LighthouseFriends ('just over three miles'), as the notes above already state.
